title: Block close: the shape of a life
hook: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love

segments.voice: Yesterday, holy laughter: Sarah's laugh behind the tent door, and then out loud for everyone to share. Your line was joy is holy. Who laughed with you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

An expert in the law steps forward with a test question for Jesus. In Matthew he asks: "Master, which is the great commandment in the law?" It's a fair question. The law is long, and a person could spend a lifetime arguing about which part matters most. He asks for one. Jesus gives him two, and then says something that gathers everything up. This block of the path has walked through Christian ethics: commandments, virtues, mercy, money, peace, the poor, the stranger, enemies, friends. Today we close it by asking what holds all of that together.

Jesus answers: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." Both lines come from the Torah, Deuteronomy and Leviticus. The first belongs to the Shema, the passage that opens with Hear, O Israel. Jesus doesn't invent a new law here; he names what the law hangs on, like a coat on a hook. Paul says the same thing his own way. In Romans he lists commandments, do not kill, do not steal, do not covet, and says they are "briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Then: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling, not canceling. Love doesn't make the commandments optional. It's what they were reaching for all along. Colossians adds a picture. After a list of virtues, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, it says: "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness." Love as the belt that holds the rest in place. Augustine, in a sermon on the first letter of John, pushed it into a short line, remembered in English as: love, and do what you will. He meant a love that sometimes says no, the way a parent does. So here is the shape of a life, as this block has traced it. Commandments as the frame. Virtues as the habits. Mercy, peace and welcome as the practice. And love underneath all of it.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three commandments for your year. Settle, and breathe. Ask what three short lines would give this year its shape. Keep them plain and doable. Call my mother on Sundays. Give before I spend. Say the hard thing kindly. Let each one be a form of love, toward God if you pray, toward a neighbor, toward the person you're becoming. Don't write yet. Just turn them over until they're short enough to remember. When the bell rings, write all three down. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of this block on Christian ethics: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love, which Paul calls the fulfilling of the law.

Your line: love fulfils it all. Today, put your three lines somewhere you'll see them, and keep one of them before the day ends. Tomorrow a new block begins: the great thinkers. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Churches teach Jesus's two great commandments, love of God and love of neighbor, as a summary of Christian ethics, and teach the commandments and virtues as ways that love takes shape in daily life.

notes: Block close for Block C (Christian ethics, days 1182–1236): the look-back list (commandments, virtues, mercy, money, peace, the poor, the stranger, enemies, friends) is drawn from the index; confirm against the finished block.
'Jews say the first one in the Shema' (Deuteronomy 6:4–9); confirm phrasing.

Augustine's 'love, and do what you will' (dilige, et quod vis fac) is paraphrased and attributed to his homilies on 1 John (7.8); confirm the reference and the gloss about love that sometimes says no (his examples of a father's correction).
Matthew 22:35 calls the questioner 'a lawyer' who asked 'tempting him'; rendered as 'an expert in the law' with 'a test question', without making the Pharisees a foil.
Index carry 'love fulfils it all' uses the British spelling 'fulfils'; kept exactly as the validator requires. Suggest 'love fulfills it all' in a separate index edit.

Editor pass: 'Jews say the first one in the Shema' (a claim about all Jews) became a statement about the text: the first line belongs to the Shema passage. Augustine's line 'usually given as' became 'remembered in English as' (claims rule).
Audit pass: "Matthew gives it word for word" (a claim about the Gospel as verbatim record) became "In Matthew he asks".
